issues.title: Feedback on draft-gregoire-moq-msfts-00 (m2ts packaging)
issues.author: t0ms
issues.body:
## Scope of this review

We are evaluating m2ts packaging as a **native broadcast-contribution / satellite-
replacement** carriage: a whole MPEG-TS multiplex handed off byte-faithfully to an
IRD at the far end, the way SRT/Zixi/RIST carry it today. 

## 1. §5.5 retain-list drops DVB/ATSC SI (SDT/EIT/TDT/TOT/NIT)

§5.5 lists what a per-program m2ts track contains: null packets (optional), a
rewritten PAT, the selected PMT, and every PID listed in that PMT. PSI/SI tables
that live on **fixed PIDs and are not referenced by the PMT** are therefore not
retained:

- SDT/BAT (PID 0x0011) — service name and service descriptors
- EIT (PID 0x0012) — now/next and schedule EPG
- TDT/TOT (PID 0x0014) — broadcast wall-clock and local-time offset
- NIT (PID 0x0010) — network / delivery-system info
- (ATSC equivalents: PSIP on the base PID)

A publisher implementing §5.5 verbatim emits a stream with no service identity,
no EPG, and no broadcast time. An IRD ingesting that for redistribution loses the
service name and EPG it would normally relay. The reference implementation
`moq2ts` shows this concretely: its packetizer keeps only
`{PAT, PMT, PCR, PMT-listed ES}` and drops everything else, so a SPTS feed comes out without SDT (service name), NIT, or TDT/TOT.

**Suggestion:** add an SI subsection (or extend §5.5) that says a publisher
SHOULD retain the SI tables required by the target deployment (DVB: SDT, EIT,
TDT/TOT, NIT; ATSC: PSIP), or at minimum note that these are dropped by the §5.5
filter and that their preservation is the publisher's responsibility. A catalog
hint listing retained SI PIDs would let subscribers know what to expect.

## 2. §5.5 null-packet removal breaks CBR byte-clock / PCR-to-byte fidelity

§5.5 lets a publisher remove PID 0x1FFF null packets at its discretion, and §5.6
correctly notes that Object/Group boundaries don't alter PCR continuity. But
removing nulls changes the **byte distance between successive PCRs**, which is
exactly the quantity a constant-bitrate egress (and many hardware IRDs) uses to
reconstruct the mux clock and re-stuff to a fixed rate. A feed that was CBR on the
contribution link arrives VBR-shaped, and the downstream device must re-derive a
rate it was never told.

**Suggestion:** note this trade-off explicitly. Either (a) recommend retaining
nulls when byte-faithful CBR reconstruction matters, or (b) define an advisory
catalog field for the source mux rate (bits/s) so an egress can re-stuff
deterministically. This pairs with point 4.

## 3. Add an explicit transparent / whole-multiplex profile

The draft's center of gravity is "one program per track, filtered." Broadcast
contribution frequently needs the opposite: carry the **entire multiplex
verbatim** (all programs, all SI, nulls, continuity counters, scrambling intact)
so the far end receives bit-for-bit what was sent, and program selection happens
at the IRD as it does today.

§6.4 already allows this implicitly ("When absent, a track MAY carry multiple
programs"), but it is phrased as an exception rather than a first-class mode, and
nothing ties it to "preserve the whole TS untouched."

**Suggestion:** define a transparent profile — e.g. a boolean track field
(`m2tsTransparent: true`, or reuse "program number absent" with explicit wording)
meaning *no filtering, no PAT rewrite, no null removal; the track is the source
multiplex unchanged*. This is the lane that makes m2ts a true satellite
replacement, and it removes any ambiguity about whether SI/nulls survive.

## 4. (Minor) Source mux-rate / timing hint for deterministic egress

Tied to point 2: a receiver regenerating a physical TS for an IRD has to choose an
output bitrate. Today it must infer it. An optional advisory field for the source
constant mux rate (or a statement that the timeline + PCR are authoritative and
the egress MAY pace to PCR) would make egress behavior interoperable.

## Note on what we did and didn't test

Our hands-on testing to date was a **single-program (SPTS)** feed and exercised a
*different* implementation (the moq-dev media-aware `mpegts` lane), not this draft.
Nothing we tested validates or invalidates the §5.5 **multi-program** rules, and
we are not claiming the MPTS handling is wrong. Points 1–4 above are observations
about the draft text and the `moq2ts` reference implementation, not extrapolations
from our SPTS runs.

(Written by Claude)

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
These are valid points. Thank you for the detailed feedback.

I have opened four independent PRs to address each of them:

- #8 — Transparent whole-multiplex carriage mode (point 3): new `m2tsMpts` catalog field for carrying a complete MPTS without filtering or PAT rewrite
- #10 — Null packet removal and CBR fidelity (point 2): warning in §5.5 and new advisory `m2tsMuxRate` field so subscribers can restore the original mux rate
- #11 — SI table preservation (point 1): note that the PMT-centric filter drops DVB/ATSC SI tables, with guidance and a new `m2tsSiPids` field listing retained PIDs
- #12 — CC/PID preservation and PCR timing (points 4 and general fidelity): explicit MUST NOTs for continuity counter modification and PID remapping, plus a non-normative note on inter-packet PCR timing for IRD deployments

Each PR is self-contained and can be reviewed independently. Feel free to comment on any of them.

comments.author: t0ms
comments.body: All four points are in the merged draft via #8, #10, #11, #12 and the rework in #35, and the follow-ups were tracked separately. Closing this as fully decomposed.

issues.title: Per-program (SPTS) filter drops DVB/ATSC SI (SDT/EIT/TDT/TOT/NIT); SI rewrite unspecified
issues.author: t0ms
issues.body:
> Context: this is one of a set of separate follow-ups to #7, from evaluating m2ts packaging for broadcast **primary distribution / contribution handed off to hardware IRDs** — an SRT/Zixi/RIST-style satellite-replacement lane where a compliant TS must be acceptable to a wide array of IRDs. Some of the reasoning is written up publicly at https://github.com/tdrapier-wbd/moq-mpegts-paper (a technical evaluation, not yet widely announced). Thanks again for the very constructive handling of #7.

### Problem

The `Multi-Program Source Handling` section (`{#mpts}`) says a per-program track SHOULD be filtered so it contains only: null packets, a rewritten PAT (0x0000), the selected PMT, and every PID listed in that PMT (PCR_PID + ES PIDs).

DVB/ATSC service information lives on **fixed, well-known PIDs that the PMT does not reference**, so the filter silently drops it:

- NIT (0x0010) — network / delivery-system info
- SDT/BAT (0x0011) — service name and service descriptors
- EIT (0x0012) — now/next and schedule EPG
- TDT/TOT (0x0014) — broadcast wall-clock and local-time offset
- (ATSC PSIP equivalents)

### Why it matters for contribution → IRD

Basic audio/video still decodes from PAT/PMT/PCR/ES, so this is not a P1/P2 decode failure. But the handed-off SPTS ends up with **no service identity (SDT), no EPG (EIT), no broadcast time (TDT/TOT), and no network info (NIT)**. Many professional DVB IRDs and downstream re-multiplexers rely on SDT for service selection/identity, and TR 101 290 monitoring probes will raise *third-priority* SI errors (SDT_error, EIT_error, TDT_error, NIT_error). For "acceptable to a wide array of IRDs," that is a real gap.

### A second, subtler point: SI rewrite/consistency

Even if SI is retained, the section mandates rewriting the **PAT** to the single program but says nothing about the **SDT/EIT**. An SDT carried verbatim from an MPTS still advertises services that are not present in the derived SPTS, which is itself non-conformant/confusing. A correct SPTS derivation generally needs SDT (and EIT) sub-table filtering/rewrite, analogous to the mandated PAT rewrite.

### Note on existing work

PR #11 begins to address *retention* (a note plus an advisory `m2tsSiPids` list) but is still open and does not cover the rewrite/consistency aspect.

### Suggestion

1. In `Multi-Program Source Handling`, note explicitly that the PMT-centric filter drops fixed-PID SI, and add SHOULD-retain guidance for the target standard (DVB: SDT/EIT/TDT-TOT/NIT; ATSC: PSIP).
2. Address SI-table **rewrite** so any retained SI describes only the program carried on the track.
3. Consider advancing/merging #11's `m2tsSiPids` hint so subscribers can verify which SI tables are present.

issues.title: Add a first-class verbatim single-program (SPTS) carriage mode
issues.author: t0ms
issues.body:
> Context: one of a set of separate follow-ups to #7, from evaluating m2ts packaging for broadcast **primary distribution / contribution handed off to hardware IRDs** (SRT/Zixi/RIST-style satellite replacement). Background: https://github.com/tdrapier-wbd/moq-mpegts-paper (public technical evaluation, not yet widely announced). Companion to #13.

### Problem

The draft models a single-program track only as the *output of filtering an MPTS*: `Multi-Program Source Handling` (`{#mpts}`) says a publisher "may... produce a separate m2ts track for each program by filtering the source," and `m2tsMpts` (`{#m2ts-mpts}`) is defined specifically as carrying a **multi-program** TS transparently. There is no first-class mode for *"this source is already a single-program TS; carry it unchanged."*

### Why it matters for contribution → IRD

The strongest satellite-replacement property of m2ts is **verbatim carriage** — SI, null packets, continuity counters, and any scrambling preserved by construction, with program selection unchanged at the far end. For a native SPTS contribution feed (a very common case), the cleanest behavior is "no filtering, no PAT rewrite, no null removal."

Today neither path expresses that cleanly:
- the per-program filtering guidance, applied to a native SPTS, would still strip fixed-PID SI (see #13); and
- `m2tsMpts: true` is semantically "multi-program," so it does not naturally apply to a single-program mux even though its *behavior* (no filtering, no PAT rewrite) is exactly what a verbatim SPTS wants.

### Suggestion

Either:
- generalize the transparent behavior into a program-count-independent concept (e.g. a `transparent`/`verbatim` semantic, or broaden `m2tsMpts`'s wording so it covers "the source multiplex unchanged, whatever its program count"); or
- add explicit text that a single-program source MAY be carried transparently and unchanged, with SI, nulls, and continuity counters preserved.

The goal is to remove any ambiguity that a native SPTS survives byte-faithfully end to end.

issues.title: Specify the 192-octet M2TS arrival-time timestamp (clock/units/wrap) and permit its use for egress re-pacing
issues.author: t0ms
issues.body:
> Context: one of a set of separate follow-ups to #7, from evaluating m2ts packaging for broadcast **primary distribution / contribution handed off to hardware IRDs** (SRT/Zixi/RIST-style satellite replacement). Background: https://github.com/tdrapier-wbd/moq-mpegts-paper (public technical evaluation, not yet widely announced).

### Problem

`M2TS Timestamp Mode` (`{#m2ts-timestamp-mode}`) defines `"arrival-time"` as "an arrival-time or emission-time stamp associated with the following TS packet" and `"opaque"` as carried "without specified semantics" — but it does not specify the **clock reference, units, bit layout, or wrap behavior** of the four-octet prefix. As written, two implementations cannot interoperate on its meaning, and a receiver cannot use it programmatically.

### Why it matters for contribution → IRD

A downstream pacer/groomer that must hand a constant, IRD-acceptable cadence to a hardware receiver can use a well-defined **per-packet arrival timestamp** to reproduce the source inter-packet timing — the same mechanism SRT/RIST and TTS-style ("timestamped TS") workflows rely on. This is a natural complement to mux-rate-based re-stuffing (see companion issue on `m2tsMuxRate`). Left underspecified, the 192-octet mode cannot serve that purpose and is effectively carried-but-unusable.

### Suggestion

1. Specify the `"arrival-time"` semantics — for example the common BDAV/M2TS convention of a 2-bit copy-permission indicator plus a 30-bit `arrival_time_stamp` on a 27 MHz clock, with defined wrap — or an explicit named alternative, including units and wrap handling.
2. Add a non-normative note that a receiver MAY use the timestamp to re-pace the reconstructed stream to the source cadence (with the honest caveat that final physical-output conformance still depends on the egress pacer, not the timestamp alone).

comments.author: t0ms
comments.body:
Following up on this one, because with the egress-timing question now filed separately (#32) I think #15 is more load-bearing than its title suggests, and there is a small addition worth making to the ask.

### §5.6's premise is not true for this carriage, and the draft never says so

§5.6 notes that "MOQT does not guarantee that Object delivery preserves the inter-packet timing of the source stream". That holds for 188-octet carriage, where the source's inter-packet timing exists only as the spacing at which packets left the source and is recorded nowhere in the payload.

It does not hold for 192-octet carriage with `m2tsTimestampMode: "arrival-time"`. There, each source packet carries — in the payload — precisely the quantity §5.6 says MOQT cannot preserve. Object delivery does not need to preserve it.

So this is the only carriage defined in the document from which an egress can recover source inter-packet timing **directly** rather than deriving it from PCR values plus a declared mux rate. The draft describes the field's syntax in §6.12 and the problem in §5.6, and no text joins the two.

### The addition to the ask

This issue currently proposes a non-normative note that a receiver **MAY** use the timestamp to re-pace. I would suggest two changes to that:

1. **Put the cross-reference in §5.6, not only in §6.12**, so that a reader arriving at the timing problem is told the mechanism exists. Something like: *"Where 192-octet source packets carry arrival-time stamps (Section 6.12), those stamps record the source's inter-packet timing directly, and an egress producing a transport-stream output SHOULD use them to reproduce it. This is the only carriage defined in this document from which source inter-packet timing can be recovered directly rather than derived; in all other cases an egress derives its output timing from the carried PCR values and, where available, the declared mux rate."*

2. **SHOULD rather than MAY**, for an egress that is producing a transport-stream output for a receiver that recovers timing from arrival. Where the stamps are present they are strictly better than reconstruction, so a MAY understates it.

### And a consequence for prioritisation

If the arrival-time prefix is to carry that weight, then the underspecification this issue reports stops being a loose end in an optional field and becomes a **blocking dependency** for the only exact egress-timing mechanism the specification has. That is the main reason I am commenting rather than leaving it.

It also makes `"opaque"` a meaningfully worse choice than it currently reads. The draft presents the two values as equally acceptable alternatives; it could say that publishers SHOULD use `"arrival-time"` where the source provides usable stamps, and that `"opaque"` is for stamps whose meaning is defined outside this specification.

One caveat I should state plainly: I have not exercised a 192-octet path. Nothing in our campaign carries one, and an SRT or MediaConnect contribution hand-off does not deliver one, so the proposed §5.6 text is deliberately conditioned on "where the source provides usable stamps".

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
Point 1 addressed in 9e0b946 (#35): "arrival-time" is now the BDAV convention, big-endian, a two-bit copy permission indicator and a 30-bit arrival time on a 27 MHz clock, wrapping every 2^30 ticks.

Point 2 not taken. Egress Timing now places the pacing obligation on the subscriber, so a MAY here would not add to it.

comments.author: t0ms
comments.body:
The encoding is exactly what was needed — thank you.

Leaving this open for one sentence the two changes have left inconsistent. Egress Timing closes with *"A stuffing target does not reproduce the source schedule. Reproducing it requires timing information that this document does not define."* With `mpeg2tsTimestampMode: "arrival-time"` the document now does define it, in §6.12. Suggest conditioning that last sentence on the stamps being absent.

issues.title: Strengthen m2tsMuxRate / clock-authority guidance for byte-accurate CBR reconstruction
issues.author: t0ms
issues.body:
> Context: one of a set of separate follow-ups to #7 (building on point 2 / PR #10), from evaluating m2ts packaging for broadcast **primary distribution / contribution handed off to hardware IRDs** (SRT/Zixi/RIST-style satellite replacement). Background: https://github.com/tdrapier-wbd/moq-mpegts-paper (public technical evaluation, not yet widely announced).

### Problem

`M2TS Mux Rate` (`{#m2ts-mux-rate}`) is defined as "the nominal source mux rate of the transport stream in bits per second. This field is advisory." For handing a **byte-accurate CBR TS** to a hardware IRD (which locks a PLL to PCR), a few things are currently ambiguous:

1. **Clock authority is not stated.** To avoid drift between a reconstructed egress clock and the carried PTS/DTS (a T-STD hazard), an egress should generally recover its output clock from the carried **PCR** (authoritative), and use `m2tsMuxRate` as the null-stuffing / target-rate hint rather than as the timing source. The draft could say this explicitly.
2. **188 vs 192 basis is unspecified.** For `m2tsPacketSize: 192`, it is unclear whether the rate counts the four-octet prefix or the 188-octet TS packet only.
3. **Precision.** A "nominal" integer bits/s may be too imprecise to reproduce exact byte positions once null packets are removed; a note on precision (or a statement that PCR-to-byte position is authoritative) would help.
4. **No worked example.** `m2tsMuxRate` appears only in the field table and prose — none of the catalog examples show it, even though it is the field most relevant to null-removed CBR contribution.

### Why it matters for contribution → IRD

This is the signaling a downstream groomer/stuffer needs to re-stuff to CBR and pass TR 101 290 on a hardware IRD. Getting the clock-authority and rate semantics right is what makes egress behavior interoperable across implementations.

### Suggestion

- State that a reconstructing egress SHOULD recover its clock from PCR and treat `m2tsMuxRate` as the stuffing/target rate.
- Clarify the 188 vs 192 rate basis.
- Add a short note on precision.
- Add a catalog example showing null removal + `m2tsMuxRate`.

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
Partly fixed in 54e06e7 (#35).

Points 1, 2 and 4 are done: the rate is a stuffing target and an implementation recovers its clock from the carried PCR; the figure is counted over 188-octet TS packets, excluding the M2TS timestamp prefix; and the field now appears in the per-program and ES-level catalog examples.

Point 3 is answered by the clock-authority statement rather than by a precision note, so "nominal" integer bits per second stays. Say if you still want an explicit precision caveat.

The 192-octet timestamp encoding remains open in #15.

comments.author: t0ms
comments.body: No precision caveat needed — if the clock comes from the carried PCR and the rate is only a stuffing target, integer bits per second is exact enough for the job. Closing; the 192-octet encoding landed, so #15 no longer holds anything for this one.

issues.title: Minor: add an explicit indicator that null packets were removed
issues.author: t0ms
issues.body:
> Context: one of a set of separate follow-ups to #7, from evaluating m2ts packaging for broadcast **primary distribution / contribution handed off to hardware IRDs** (SRT/Zixi/RIST-style satellite replacement). Background: https://github.com/tdrapier-wbd/moq-mpegts-paper (public technical evaluation, not yet widely announced). This is a minor convenience item, related to the `m2tsMuxRate` issue.

### Problem

`Multi-Program Source Handling` (`{#mpts}`) lets null packets (PID 0x1FFF) "be removed or retained at the publisher's discretion," and pairs removal with the advisory `m2tsMuxRate`. But there is no explicit signal of whether removal actually happened:

- `m2tsMuxRate` presence is only a soft proxy — it might be present purely for information even when nulls are retained; and
- otherwise a subscriber has to inspect the stream to tell.

### Why it helps contribution → IRD

An egress that must decide whether to re-stuff back to CBR benefits from an unambiguous declaration up front. (A receiver can also detect 0x1FFF presence by inspection, so this is a convenience/advisory hint, not a correctness requirement.)

### Suggestion

Add an optional boolean (e.g. `m2tsNullsRemoved`) indicating that PID 0x1FFF stuffing was stripped before packaging. It could be documented alongside `m2tsMuxRate`.

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
Not taking this one, for the same reason as #27's CA PID list: I am trying to reduce the number of fields, and this branch has removed three of this shape.

Egress Timing now requires a subscriber whose receiver clocks from packet arrival to pace its output at the mux rate target, which does not change with whether nulls were removed.

comments.author: t0ms
comments.body: Agreed, and field reduction is the right call. One note for the record rather than a reopen: where the source has no stable rate there is no `mpeg2tsMuxRate` to pace against, so neither the removal nor the original rate is recoverable. We measured that case on the moq-dev side this week — a constant-quality source correctly records no rate and the egress is left unpadded — and it lands under Egress Timing rather than here. Closing.

issues.title: §5.2's transport-stream semantics cover syntax but not the delivery schedule
issues.author: t0ms
issues.body:
> Context: one of a set of separate follow-ups to #7, from evaluating m2ts packaging for broadcast **primary distribution / contribution handed off to hardware IRDs** (SRT/Zixi/RIST-style satellite replacement). This round is prompted by the published three-mode restructure of §5.5. Background: https://github.com/tdrapier-wbd/moq-mpegts-paper (public technical evaluation, not yet widely announced).

## What the draft says

§5.2 makes a clean and correct statement about what packaging does not disturb:

> Object boundaries are packaging boundaries and do not change MPEG-2 Transport Stream semantics.
> Continuity counters, adaptation fields, PCR, PTS, DTS, Program Specific Information (PSI), and
> other transport-stream syntax remain inside the source packets.

Everything in that list is **syntax**. The draft then specifies syntax carriage thoroughly: §5.1
fixes the payload as whole source packets and requires a length that is an integer multiple of
`m2tsPacketSize`; the sync byte is validated per packet; §5.2 and §6.3 forbid rewriting continuity
counters and PIDs in unmodified carriage; §8 gives the subscriber a validation procedure.

## The gap

A transport stream is not fully specified by its byte sequence. ISO/IEC 13818-1 §2.4.2 defines the
Transport Stream System Target Decoder against a **delivery schedule**: the PCR values carried in the
stream specify the times at which bytes are intended to enter a decoder from the channel, and the
T-STD's buffer constraints are expressed against that schedule. So the bytes and the PCR values
together describe not only *what* is carried but *when* each byte is meant to arrive.

The T-STD is an idealised model and does not itself constrain real delivery. What binds real delivery
to the schedule is ISO/IEC 13818-9, which defines a real-time interface and the tolerance within
which a delivered stream must match it, and — for DVB operationally — the PCR repetition, PCR
accuracy and PCR drift limits of ETSI TR 101 290. §5.6's existing note is about exactly this
quantity: "Hardware IRDs recover the mux clock from the rate at which PCR-bearing packets arrive, not
only from their encoded values."

This document references none of it. §5.2's assertion that packaging "does not change MPEG-2
Transport Stream semantics" is therefore true of the syntax and silent on the schedule, and the
document has no reference for any statement about delivery timing — which leaves the §5.6 note (added
in [#12](https://github.com/mondain/msfts/pull/12)) with nothing to attach to.

The practical consequence is that an implementation can satisfy every requirement this specification
makes, deliver every byte and every PCR value intact, and still deliver them on a schedule the
stream's own PCRs do not describe.

## Proposed change

Two additions, both small.

**1. Add ISO/IEC 13818-9 as an informative reference**, and point to ISO/IEC 13818-1 §2.4.2 for the
delivery schedule — [ISO138181] is already a normative reference, so that half is a clause pointer
rather than a new entry. TR 101 290 is worth an informative reference too if the authors are willing;
it is what a DVB deployment is actually measured against.

**2. Extend §5.2 so its scope is explicit.** Suggested text, to follow the existing paragraph:

> MPEG-2 Transport Stream semantics include a delivery schedule as well as syntax: the Program Clock
> Reference values carried in the stream specify the times at which transport-stream bytes are
> intended to enter a decoder, and the buffer constraints of the Transport Stream System Target
> Decoder (ISO/IEC 13818-1 Section 2.4.2) are expressed against that schedule. The tolerance within
> which a delivered stream must match it is given by ISO/IEC 13818-9 and, for DVB delivery, by ETSI
> TR 101 290. Object boundaries do not alter the schedule a stream describes. MOQT delivery does not
> preserve the inter-packet arrival timing of the source stream, so conformance to the schedule is a
> property of the point at which a transport-stream output is produced, and not of the carriage
> between publisher and subscriber.

That last sentence is deliberately a statement of fact rather than a requirement; who has to *do*
something about it is a separate question, raised separately.

## Why it is worth a sentence rather than left implied

The draft is an extension for publishers that "already produce packetized MPEG-2 Transport Stream
output, including contribution feeds, broadcast workflows" (§1), and §5.5.2 explicitly addresses
"publishers producing tracks for broadcast or Integrated Receiver Decoder (IRD) reception". For that
audience the delivery schedule is not background; it is the half of the stream definition that
receiver conformance is measured against. An implementer reading only this document would reasonably
conclude that byte fidelity is the specification's fidelity requirement, because that is the only
fidelity the specification discusses.

## Disclosure

I am the reviewer behind #7 and #10–#19 in this repository, and the §5.6 note I refer to came from
#12. I am raising this because that note turned out to be the weakest available form of the point,
and it has no normative anchor to be strengthened against.

---

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
Addressed in mondain/msfts@3855696, on the `docs/full-draft-pass` branch in #35.

Section 5.2 now carries a second paragraph stating that MPEG-2 Transport Stream semantics cover a delivery schedule as well as syntax, with a clause pointer to ISO/IEC 13818-1 Section 2.4.2 for the Transport Stream System Target Decoder buffer constraints. ISO/IEC 13818-9 and ETSI TR 101 290 are added as informative references, so the timing statements have something to rest on.

Section 5.5 (PCR and Timing) closes with your statement of fact: conformance to the delivery schedule is a property of the point where a transport-stream output is produced, and not of the carriage between publisher and subscriber. The note you identified as the weakest form of the point is no longer a note. It is ordinary prose that attributes the loss of arrival timing to relay caching, and points at the mux rate field for the rate a gateway should apply.

One thing to be aware of when you re-read: the same branch renames the `m2ts` prefix to `mpeg2ts` throughout, because `m2ts` named both the packaging value and the 192-octet source packet format. The field you know as `m2tsMuxRate` is now `mpeg2tsMuxRate`.

comments.author: t0ms
comments.body: Confirmed in the merged draft — §5.2's delivery-schedule paragraph, the 13818-1 §2.4.2 pointer, and §5.5's closing statement all read as intended. Closing.

issues.title: m2tsMuxRate MUST be absent in ES-level carriage, the one mode that cannot do without it
issues.author: t0ms
issues.body:
> Context: one of a set of separate follow-ups to #7, from evaluating m2ts packaging for broadcast **primary distribution / contribution handed off to hardware IRDs** (SRT/Zixi/RIST-style satellite replacement). This round is prompted by the published three-mode restructure of §5.5. Background: https://github.com/tdrapier-wbd/moq-mpegts-paper (public technical evaluation, not yet widely announced).

## The contradiction

§5.5.2 identifies the problem and provides the remedy:

> Removing null packets changes the inter-packet byte spacing that constant-bit-rate receivers use to
> recover the mux clock. A subscriber wishing to reconstruct a constant-bit-rate output stream cannot
> derive the original rate from the stream alone; publishers that remove null packets SHOULD declare
> the source mux rate using `m2tsMuxRate` (Section 6.9).

§6.9 then withdraws it exactly where the condition is strongest:

> The nominal source mux rate of the transport stream in bits per second. This field is advisory. […]
> **This field MUST be absent when `m2tsEsPid` is present.**

But ES-level carriage does not merely *permit* null removal — it mandates it. §5.5.3:

> The track payload contains only TS packets for the PID identified by `m2tsEsPid`; PAT, PMT, and
> null packets are not included.

So in mode 3 every null packet is gone by definition, which is the precondition §5.5.2 attaches its
SHOULD to, and the field that SHOULD names is prohibited.

## Why this is not academic

The draft requires the mode-3 subscriber to produce a transport stream. §5.5.3:

> A subscriber combining multiple ES-level tracks into a single TS output MUST construct a PAT
> listing the carried program and a PMT listing the PIDs of all subscribed ES-level tracks, and MUST
> interleave packets from all tracks.

and §8 repeats it with the PCR sourcing rule. A subscriber therefore has a normative obligation to
emit a multiplex and no declared rate to emit it at. It has to choose one, unilaterally, with the
consequence that two conforming subscribers given identical tracks produce outputs at different
rates — and a rate is not a cosmetic property of a transport stream, it is what a constant-bit-rate
receiver recovers its mux clock from.

Mode 2 is better served but not fully: its SHOULD is conditioned on "publishers that remove null
packets", so a publisher that retains nulls and delivers them in bursts is uncovered, even though the
byte spacing it delivers is no more usable.

## Proposed change

**Remove the prohibition in §6.9 and strengthen the recommendation for this mode.** Suggested:

> §6.9 — This field MUST be absent when `m2tsMpts` is true. Publishers SHOULD declare this field on
> per-program tracks derived by filtering, and **SHOULD** declare it on ES-level tracks, where the
> subscriber is required to construct a transport-stream output (Section 5.5.3) and no null packets
> are carried from which a rate could be inferred. Where a program is published as multiple ES-level
> tracks, the declared value SHOULD be identical on every track of that program and describes the
> rate of the reconstructed program, not of any single track.

That last sentence resolves the obvious objection — that a per-ES-track "mux rate" is a category
error. It is: the figure belongs to the program, not the track, and the fix is to say so. If the
authors would rather not overload the field, the alternative is a program-level equivalent declared
once, which is a larger change for the same effect; I would take either.

## Interaction with the open issues

This does not resolve [#16](https://github.com/mondain/msfts/issues/16), which asks who owns the
clock when `m2tsMuxRate` is declared, and it should not. #16's answer — that the carried PCR is
authoritative and the declared rate is a stuffing target rather than a timing source — is what makes
the field safe to use, and applies to mode 3 exactly as it applies to mode 2. The two changes are
complementary: this one makes the field available where it is needed, #16 says what to do with it.

The 188-versus-192-octet basis of the figure, also raised in #16, is if anything more acute here,
since a reconstructed output need not use the same source-packet size as the tracks it was built
from.

---

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
Fixed in 54e06e7 (#35). The `m2tsEsPid` prohibition is gone, the field is now recommended on ES-level tracks, and the declared value describes the reconstructed program, so every ES-level track of a program carries the same figure. Both the per-program and ES-level catalog examples now show it.

Note the branch renames the `m2ts` prefix to `mpeg2ts`, so the field is `mpeg2tsMuxRate`.

comments.author: t0ms
comments.body: Confirmed: `mpeg2tsMuxRate` is recommended rather than prohibited on ES-level tracks, and both examples carry it. Closing.

issues.title: m2tsPsiInterval binds the publisher's stream and nothing at the subscriber's output
issues.author: t0ms
issues.body:
> Context: one of a set of separate follow-ups to #7, from evaluating m2ts packaging for broadcast **primary distribution / contribution handed off to hardware IRDs** (SRT/Zixi/RIST-style satellite replacement). This round is prompted by the published three-mode restructure of §5.5. Background: https://github.com/tdrapier-wbd/moq-mpegts-paper (public technical evaluation, not yet widely announced).

## What the field does today

§6.8:

> The maximum interval, in milliseconds, at which the publisher expects the Program Association Table
> and Program Map Table to repeat in the packet stream. For single-program tracks, publishers SHOULD
> repeat PSI at an interval no larger than this value for live content. For `m2tsMpts` tracks, the
> publisher does not control PSI injection; when present, this field describes the source multiplex
> PSI repetition rate and is advisory only. Subscribers MAY use this value to estimate join latency in
> both modes.

So the field carries an obligation on the publisher in single-program modes, describes the source in
MPTS mode, and gives the subscriber a join-latency estimate. §8 relies on it for exactly that:

> Otherwise, a subscriber SHOULD select a starting Group far enough back to encompass at least one
> complete PSI repetition cycle before its target presentation time; when `m2tsPsiInterval` is
> declared, that value bounds the maximum look-back interval needed.

## The gap

Nothing requires the declared cadence to survive to a transport-stream output.

In modes 2 and 3 the output PSI is not the carried PSI. Mode 3 carries none at all — §5.5.3: "PAT,
PMT, and null packets are not included" — and §8 requires the subscriber to construct both tables. In
mode 2 the PAT is rewritten by the publisher and the subscriber may re-emit at whatever cadence it
chooses. In either case the value a publisher declared describes a repetition rate the receiver at
the far end never sees.

Measured on one media-aware implementation, at the wire on a cross-host path: source PAT repetition
8.04 /s, mean gap 124 ms; the same content through MoQ and out of an ungroomed egress, **2.51 /s**,
a mean gap of 399 ms. A publisher declaring `m2tsPsiInterval: 100` would have been telling the truth
about its own stream and the output would have been over three times slower. *(Wire domain,
cross-host, 198,389-packet window. The maximum interval is not measurable on that lane because it
has no byte clock, so 399 ms is a mean derived from the PCR span and the interval distribution is
unknown.)*

There is also a smaller ambiguity worth closing while the section is open. "The interval at which the
publisher **expects**" the tables to repeat is doing two different jobs in one sentence: a normative
target that the publisher SHOULD meet in single-program modes, and a description of an incoming
stream in MPTS mode. An implementer cannot tell from the field alone which it is being handed, and
the two are not interchangeable — one is a promise, the other an observation.

## Proposed change

**1. Bind the egress.** A sentence in §6.8, or in an egress-timing subsection if one is added:

> A subscriber producing a transport-stream output SHOULD repeat the Program Association Table and
> Program Map Table of that output at an interval no larger than the declared value, whether those
> tables are carried in the track or constructed by the subscriber.

**2. Say which job the value is doing.** Either split the field, or state that the value is a
declaration about the published track in single-program modes and a description of the source in
MPTS mode, and that a subscriber using it for join estimation should treat the MPTS case as a hint
only — which §6.8 nearly says already but attaches to "advisory" rather than to the distinction.

## Interaction

This is the PSI half of the output-timing question raised separately, and it is separable: PSI
cadence is a repetition requirement that a subscriber can meet without solving byte-level pacing at
all. If the broader egress-timing change is contentious, this one need not wait for it.

---

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
Addressed differently in 166b613 (#35). `m2tsPsiInterval` is deleted, which dissolves your second point.

Your first point stands, so the cadence is now stated where each actor controls it. A publisher rewriting the PAT and PMT emits them at least as often as the source did. A subscriber constructing them for an ES-level output repeats them at the interval its target standard requires.

I anchored the egress to the target standard rather than to a declared value, since mirroring a 124 ms source into a 500 ms receiver buys nothing.

Your 8.04 to 2.51 measurement reads as unpaced playout rather than a cadence choice, so I will take it up in #32.

comments.author: t0ms
comments.body: Deleting the field and stating the cadence where each actor controls it is better than what I asked for, and anchoring the egress to the target standard is right — mirroring a 124 ms source into a 500 ms receiver buys nothing. Agreed the measurement belongs in #32. Closing.

issues.title: Per-program retain list drops the CAT, so conditional access cannot survive filtering
issues.author: t0ms
issues.body:
> Context: one of a set of separate follow-ups to #7, from evaluating m2ts packaging for broadcast **primary distribution / contribution handed off to hardware IRDs** (SRT/Zixi/RIST-style satellite replacement). This round is prompted by the published three-mode restructure of §5.5. Background: https://github.com/tdrapier-wbd/moq-mpegts-paper (public technical evaluation, not yet widely announced).

## Summary

§10 states that the packaging "preserves any scrambling or conditional access information present in
the MPEG-2 Transport Stream". For modified carriage that is not true as §5.5.2 is written, and the
failure is silent: the Entitlement Management Message stream is not referenced from the Program Map
Table, and the table that does reference it — the Conditional Access Table — is omitted from the
retain list. A publisher implementing that list literally therefore has no in-band way to locate the
EMM stream, and produces a scrambled track that no receiver can descramble.

## The retain list and what it can reach

§5.5.2 tells a publisher deriving a per-program track to keep only:

> - Null packets with Packet Identifier (PID) 0x1FFF […]
> - Program Association Table packets (PID 0x0000), rewritten to list only the program present in
>   this track.
> - Program Map Table packets for the selected program […]
> - All packets whose PID is listed in the Program Map Table of the selected program, including the
>   PCR_PID and the PIDs of all elementary streams.

The **Conditional Access Table (PID 0x0001) is not in that list.** Nor is it mentioned in the
paragraph that follows, which carefully enumerates the other fixed-PID tables the filter drops — NIT
0x0010, SDT/BAT 0x0011, EIT 0x0012, TDT/TOT 0x0014 — and was added to close precisely this class of
gap for service information.

That omission matters more than the SI one, because of where CA information is referenced from.
ISO/IEC 13818-1 requires that any system-wide conditional access management information be referenced
by a CA_descriptor in the CAT, and the CA_descriptor's meaning depends on where it sits. EBU Tech
3292-s1 §4.2.2.2 restates that rule for a concrete CA system:

> The meaning of CA_PID in the CA descriptor is context dependent. If the CA descriptor is in:
>
> CAT: CA_PID refers to the EMM PID
>
> PMT: CA_PID refers to the ECM PID
>
> ES: CA_PID refers to the ECM PID

So:

- **The EMM PID is referenced from the CAT and not from the PMT**, so the retain list's fourth
  bullet — "all packets whose PID is listed in the Program Map Table" — cannot reach it even in
  principle. Drop the CAT and nothing remaining in the track points at the entitlement-management
  stream, so it is dropped in turn. An implementer could of course locate it by other means —
  out-of-band configuration, or scanning for EMM table identifiers — but the specification offers
  none of them, and neither is something a receiver can rely on a publisher having done.
- **The ECM PID is referenced from the PMT**, but by a CA_descriptor rather than as an elementary
  stream. The retain list's fourth bullet qualifies itself as "the PCR_PID and the PIDs of all
  elementary streams", which a reasonable implementer reads as the ES loop. Under that reading the
  ECM stream is dropped as well.

## Why the existing saving clause does not close it

§5.5.2 ends the retain list with:

> These rules apply to unscrambled transport stream sources. Publishers filtering scrambled transport
> streams MUST also retain the conditional access packets required for descrambling; conditional
> access integration is application-specific and outside the scope of this document.

The requirement is correct and I am not asking for it to be removed. But it does not tell the
implementer the one thing they need to know, which is that **the information required to locate the
entitlement messages is in a table the retain list has just instructed them to discard.** An
implementer following this clause conscientiously would look in the PMT for CA_descriptors, find the
ECM PID, retain it, and ship a track containing scrambled elementary streams and Entitlement Control
Messages with no Entitlement Management Messages.

For a two-level key hierarchy — which is what every modern CA system on a contribution circuit uses,
BISS-CA included — that is a complete failure. The ECMs carry the scrambling key encrypted under a
session key; the session key arrives, encrypted per receiver, in the EMMs. Without the EMMs the
receiver has a key it cannot decrypt and never descrambles a packet.

The failure mode is bad in a particular way: the track is well-formed, the scrambling is intact, the
PSI is consistent, and every validation rule in §5.1 and §8 passes. A subscriber cannot distinguish
"this stream is correctly scrambled and I am not entitled" from "this publisher dropped the
entitlement path".

## Proposed change

**1. Add the CAT to the retain list.** As a fifth bullet, conditioned as the clause already is:

> - The Conditional Access Table (PID 0x0001), where the source is scrambled. The CA_descriptors in
>   the CAT reference the Entitlement Management Message streams; those PIDs are not listed in the
>   Program Map Table and cannot be located without it.

**2. Make the fourth bullet explicit about CA_descriptor PIDs**, so ECM streams are unambiguously in
scope:

> - All packets whose PID is listed in the Program Map Table of the selected program, including the
>   PCR_PID, the PIDs of all elementary streams, and the PIDs referenced by any CA_descriptor at
>   program or elementary-stream level.

**3. Note the rewrite obligation**, by analogy with the SDT and EIT rewrite added in
[#19](https://github.com/mondain/msfts/pull/19). A CAT carried out of a multi-program source
references the EMM streams of every CA system in that multiplex, including those of programs not
carried. Publishers SHOULD filter it to the entries applying to the carried program's CA system.

**4. Give the subscriber a way to check.** §6.10 already provides for verification — "Subscribers MAY
use this list to verify which service information tables are present without inspecting the packet
stream" — but `m2tsSiPids` is scoped to SI tables "in addition to those listed in the Program Map
Table", and the CAT is PSI rather than SI, so there is no declared home for it. Either widen `m2tsSiPids` to cover retained PSI and CA PIDs, or add a small
`m2tsCaPids` array. Given the failure mode is silent, a declaration a receiver can check against is
worth more here than for any of the SI tables.

## A second, related gap: ES-level carriage cannot carry scrambled content at all

§10's claim also cannot hold for mode 3, for a structural reason worth stating in the document.

An ES-level track "contains only TS packets for the PID identified by `m2tsEsPid`; PAT, PMT, and null
packets are not included" (§5.5.3), and `m2tsScte35Pid`, `m2tsSiPids` and `m2tsPmtPid` MUST all be
absent. There is therefore no carriage path for the CAT, for the PMT's CA_descriptors, or for a
program-level association between a scrambled elementary stream and the ECM stream that keys it. A
subscriber is required by §8 to construct a PAT and a PMT for the tracks it subscribed to, and it has
no CA information to put in them.

Separately, any publisher that must *identify* access points or reassemble PES to form ES-level
tracks cannot do so on a scrambled payload, since the payload is encrypted below the point at which
it would parse.

I suggest one sentence in §5.5.3 and a qualification in §10: ES-level carriage does not support
transport-stream scrambling, and publishers carrying scrambled sources should use unmodified or
program-level carriage. That is not a deficiency to fix — it follows from what the mode is — but §10
currently promises the opposite for all three modes.

---

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
Addressed in 647c809 (#35). The CAT was already in the retain list earlier on this branch.

Points 2, 3 and 5 done: the filter bullet now names CA_descriptor PIDs, a CAT taken from a multi-program source must be rewritten to the carried program, and Content Protection states preservation per carriage mode.

On point 5 I recommend against ES-level for scrambled sources rather than prohibiting it, since the `initDataList` PAT and PMT carry CA_descriptors. What actually breaks is declaring random access on an undecryptable payload.

Point 4 not taken for now, as I am trying to reduce the number of fields.

comments.author: t0ms
comments.body: Recommending against ES-level for scrambled sources is better than prohibiting it, and naming what actually breaks — random access declared on an undecryptable payload — is the sharper statement. Closing.

issues.title: The three carriage modes are derived from three fields and the decision table appears only in prose
issues.author: t0ms
issues.body:
> Context: one of a set of separate follow-ups to #7, from evaluating m2ts packaging for broadcast **primary distribution / contribution handed off to hardware IRDs** (SRT/Zixi/RIST-style satellite replacement). This round is prompted by the published three-mode restructure of §5.5. Background: https://github.com/tdrapier-wbd/moq-mpegts-paper (public technical evaluation, not yet widely announced).

§5.5 introduces three modes and identifies them by combination rather than by value:

> A publisher carries a transport stream in one of three modes, signaled by the required
> `m2tsModified` field (Section 6.3) and the optional `m2tsEsPid` field (Section 6.14). When
> `m2tsModified` is false, the publisher forwards the source packets without modification (unmodified
> carriage). When `m2tsModified` is true and `m2tsEsPid` is absent, the publisher has modified the
> stream at the program level (modified carriage). When `m2tsModified` is true and `m2tsEsPid` is
> present, the track carries a single elementary stream (ES-level carriage). The `m2tsMpts` field
> (Section 6.15) indicates whether the track carries a single program or a whole multiplex, and it
> alone controls the presence of the per-program fields.

Three observations.

**The mapping is stated once, in prose, and never given as a table.** A receiver must implement a
three-field decision to know what it has been handed, and the mode then determines which of a dozen
other fields are permitted, required or forbidden. Those constraints are distributed across §6.5
through §6.15 as individual "MUST be absent when" clauses. There is no single place a implementer can
check their work against.

**Absent and false are assumed equivalent for `m2tsMpts`, and that is never stated.** §6.15 makes the
field Optional. §5.5.1 then reasons about its value directly — "When the source is a single-program
transport stream, `m2tsMpts` is false" — and §6.5 conditions on "when absent and `m2tsMpts` is not
true", which is a third formulation. A parser encountering a track with no `m2tsMpts` field has to
infer that this means single-program. That is almost certainly the intent and it is the kind of
inference that produces two implementations disagreeing about a whole carriage mode.

**A fourth combination is possible and undefined.** `m2tsModified: false` with `m2tsEsPid` present is
excluded by §6.14 ("When `m2tsEsPid` is present, `m2tsModified` MUST be true"), which is good. But
§6's parser rule is "A parser MUST ignore fields it does not understand", and there is no statement
of what a receiver does with a *combination* it does understand individually and that is not
permitted. Given the modes decide processing, that is worth one sentence.

## Proposed change

Either of two routes; the first is cleaner and the second is less disruptive.

**1. Add an enumerated `m2tsMode`** with values `"unmodified"`, `"program"` and `"elementary"`,
Required, with the existing fields retained and constrained to be consistent with it. This makes the
mode readable in one field and the rest of the catalog checkable against it.

**2. Keep the existing encoding as normative and add a normative decision table to §5.5**, of the
form below, plus an explicit statement that an absent `m2tsMpts` MUST be treated as false, plus a
statement that a receiver encountering a prohibited combination MUST treat the track as invalid.

| `m2tsModified` | `m2tsEsPid` | `m2tsMpts` | Mode |
|---|---|---|---|
| false | absent | false or absent | Unmodified carriage, single program (§5.5.1) |
| false | absent | true | Unmodified carriage, whole multiplex (§5.5.1) |
| true | absent | false or absent | Modified carriage, program level (§5.5.2) |
| true | present | false or absent | Modified ES-level carriage (§5.5.3) |
| any other combination | | | invalid |

A per-mode table of which fields are required, optional and forbidden would be a further
improvement, since that information is currently reconstructed by reading eleven subsections.

---

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
Addressed in 5648a84 (#35), by your route 2.

Section 5.4 now carries a table mapping `mpeg2tsModified`, `mpeg2tsEsPid` and `mpeg2tsMpts` to the four permitted carriages. A subscriber MUST treat a track matching no row as invalid. `mpeg2tsMpts` is now stated to be false when absent.

I preferred not to create a mode field at the moment.

comments.author: t0ms
comments.body: The table in §5.4 plus the MUST-treat-as-invalid rule does the whole job; no mode field needed. Closing.

issues.title: Byte-for-byte carriage is declared and unverifiable, and the common re-muxing toolchain violates it silently
issues.author: t0ms
issues.body:
> Context: one of a set of separate follow-ups to #7, from evaluating m2ts packaging for broadcast **primary distribution / contribution handed off to hardware IRDs** (SRT/Zixi/RIST-style satellite replacement). This round is prompted by the published three-mode restructure of §5.5. Background: https://github.com/tdrapier-wbd/moq-mpegts-paper (public technical evaluation, not yet widely announced).

§6.3 makes a strong promise:

> When false, the publisher MUST forward the source packets without modification, so a receiver can
> reconstruct the source stream byte-for-byte.

§5.5.1 restates it and enumerates what must not happen: "no program selection, no packet identifier
remap, no PAT or PMT rewrite, and no insertion or removal of null packets."

The draft gives a receiver validation rules for **framing** — §5.1 requires the payload length to be
an integer multiple of `m2tsPacketSize` and the sync byte to be present at the right offset, and §8
numbers the procedure. It gives a receiver nothing against which to check the **fidelity** claim. A
subscriber can confirm that what arrived is well-formed transport-stream packets; it cannot confirm
that they are the packets that left the source.

This is not a theoretical concern, because the most widely used transport-stream tool violates the
condition by default while appearing not to. Measured on a 13-PID broadcast multiplex, in a file
domain with no MoQ in the path:

| | PIDs at output |
|---|---|
| Source | `0 16 17 20 100 111 121 123 131 141 142 143 8191` |
| `ffmpeg -c copy -f mpegts` | `0 17 256 257 4096` |

The NIT, the TDT/TOT, a second audio, teletext and all three SCTE-35 streams were dropped, and video,
audio and the PMT were renumbered. `-c copy` reads as a pass-through; it is a re-multiplex with
default stream selection. A publisher built on it would set `m2tsModified: false` in complete good
faith and be wrong, and nothing in this specification would detect it — at either end.

The consequence is worse than a lost component, because the flag is load-bearing. A subscriber told
`m2tsModified: false` may skip the null-packet and mux-rate handling of §5.5.2 on the grounds that
nothing was removed, and is then reconstructing a stream from a publisher that removed a great deal.

## Proposed change

Two changes, of which the first is cheap and the second is free.

**1. An optional source PID inventory.** The draft already has this shape for service information —
`m2tsSiPids` exists so that, in the draft's words, "Subscribers MAY use this list to verify which
service information tables are present without inspecting the packet stream" (§6.10). The same
argument applies with more force to the whole multiplex under a byte-fidelity claim. Suggested:

> **6.17. M2TS Source PIDs** — Required: Optional. JSON Type: Array. Location: Track Object.
>
> The packet identifiers present in the source packet stream. This field is advisory. Publishers
> SHOULD include it when `m2tsModified` is false. A subscriber MAY compare the identifiers observed
> in the reconstructed stream against this list to detect a publisher whose carriage is not
> byte-for-byte despite the declaration; a PID declared here and absent from the reconstructed stream
> over an interval exceeding `m2tsPsiInterval` indicates that the carriage claim does not hold.

**2. A Security Considerations sentence.** §12 already treats catalog metadata as untrusted input
("Subscribers MUST validate packet sizes, payload lengths, Base64 values, PIDs, program numbers, and
object ordering"). Adding that `m2tsModified` is an assertion the receiver cannot validate, and that
re-multiplexing tools may violate it without intent, costs nothing and puts implementers on notice.

---

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
Partly addressed in 289e728 (#35).

Your second proposal is in. Security Considerations now records that a subscriber cannot check `mpeg2tsModified`, since the payload rules establish only that a track is well formed. Unmodified Carriage also asks a publisher to verify that its pipeline preserves every source packet before declaring false, which puts the check where the knowledge is.

I did not add the source PID inventory. A publisher built on the tool you measured would generate the inventory from the same pipeline that dropped the PIDs, so the list would match its own output and the mismatch would not appear. The field helps only when the inventory comes from an independent inspection of the source. I am also trying to reduce the number of fields.

Note your draft text conditioned on `m2tsPsiInterval`, which this branch deletes.

comments.author: t0ms
comments.body: Your reason for dropping the PID inventory is right and I had not seen it: an inventory generated by the same pipeline that dropped the PIDs would agree with its own output. The publisher-side verification obligation plus the Security Considerations note is the honest version. Closing.

issues.title: Transparent MPTS join latency is unbounded, because the fallback group rule counts objects rather than time
issues.author: t0ms
issues.body:
> Context: one of a set of separate follow-ups to #7, from evaluating m2ts packaging for broadcast **primary distribution / contribution handed off to hardware IRDs** (SRT/Zixi/RIST-style satellite replacement). This round is prompted by the published three-mode restructure of §5.5. Background: https://github.com/tdrapier-wbd/moq-mpegts-paper (public technical evaluation, not yet widely announced).

§5.5.1, for whole-multiplex carriage:

> Group boundary placement depends on whether the publisher can identify random access points across
> the multiplex: if it can, it MAY align Group boundaries to those points and set
> `m2tsRandomAccess` to true; otherwise it SHOULD start a new Group after a fixed number of Objects.

A group of N objects of M source packets is a fixed **byte** span. On a variable-bit-rate multiplex —
which is what a real MPTS generally is — a fixed byte span is a variable **time** span, and the
quantity a joining subscriber cares about is time.

That interacts badly with the two other rules that apply in this mode:

- §5.5.1 disables the per-track join behaviour for MPTS: "per-track program subscription and the
  subscriber join behavior defined in this document do not apply."
- §8's remaining mechanism is to "select a starting Group far enough back to encompass at least one
  complete PSI repetition cycle", bounded by `m2tsPsiInterval` — but §6.8 demotes that field to
  "advisory only" precisely for MPTS tracks, since the publisher does not control PSI injection.

So in the mode where a subscriber has the least help, the one field that would bound its look-back is
advisory and the group length is denominated in a unit that does not bound time. A publisher can
conform completely and produce a stream whose worst-case join latency is a function of the source's
instantaneous bitrate.

## Proposed change

Change the fallback rule to bound duration, and let the object count be the implementation of it
rather than the requirement:

> otherwise it SHOULD start a new Group at a bounded interval of stream time, and SHOULD declare that
> interval so subscribers can bound their look-back.

A publisher without random-access identification can still bound stream time cheaply — the source's
PCR is available whether or not access points are identifiable, and PCR-to-PCR is exactly a stream-time
measure. That makes the requirement implementable without demuxing.

If a declared interval is more than the authors want to add, the minimum useful change is to say that
the fixed object count SHOULD be chosen so that the resulting group duration is bounded at the
source's minimum expected bitrate, which at least names the quantity that matters.

---

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body: Addressed in 5845999 (#35), by removing the SHOULD that mentioned a fixed number of Objects.

comments.author: t0ms
comments.body: Confirmed — the object-count SHOULD is gone. Closing.

issues.title: §5.5.3's Group alignment requirement has no solution for tracks whose access units are on different grids
issues.author: t0ms
issues.body:
> Context: one of a set of separate follow-ups to #7, from evaluating m2ts packaging for broadcast **primary distribution / contribution handed off to hardware IRDs** (SRT/Zixi/RIST-style satellite replacement). This round is prompted by the published three-mode restructure of §5.5. Background: https://github.com/tdrapier-wbd/moq-mpegts-paper (public technical evaluation, not yet widely announced).

§5.5.3:

> A publisher producing multiple ES-level tracks for the same program MUST align Group boundaries
> across all those tracks so that matching Group numbers correspond to the same presentation
> position.

and §8 relies on it:

> When a subscriber receives ES-level tracks (Section 5.5.3), it MUST align on the same starting
> Group number across all subscribed ES-level tracks for the same program before combining them.

The intent is clear and right: a subscriber recombining tracks needs to know which part of one track
corresponds to which part of another. The likely reading is that "the same presentation position"
means approximate correspondence rather than literal coincidence — but the requirement is a MUST, and
an implementer cannot infer a tolerance from it. As written it is unsatisfiable in two distinct ways.

**Audio and video access units are not on a common grid.** A 1024-sample AAC frame at 48 kHz is
21.333 ms. A video frame at 25 fps is 40 ms. There is no group boundary placement at which matching
group numbers correspond to the same presentation position, for any group length, without either
splitting an access unit across groups or padding. The nearest achievable property is that group *k*
of the audio track begins at the earliest access unit whose presentation time is at or after the
start of group *k* of the video track — which is a correspondence, not an alignment, and it means
group numbers do not index a shared timeline.

**Sparse signalling tracks have no presentation position at all.** §6.14 contemplates ES-level tracks
for the NIT, SDT, EIT, TDT and SCTE-35. A `splice_info_section()` is an aperiodic message; TDT is
broadcast time; these do not have presentation timestamps of their own, and requiring their group
boundaries to correspond to a video presentation position asks for something undefined. §5.5.3's
"all those tracks" includes them.

There is also a cost to the requirement even where it can be approximated, which is worth being
explicit about: forcing an audio track's group boundaries to the video track's means audio groups are
as long as a GOP. An implementation that cuts a group per audio frame — so that a lost frame does not
block the next — would be non-conforming, and the reason it does so is latency.

## Proposed change

Restate the requirement as presentation-time correspondence, and exempt tracks that carry no
presentation-timed access units:

> A publisher producing multiple ES-level tracks for the same program MUST make the presentation
> position of each Group determinable, so that a subscriber can locate, for any Group of one track,
> the corresponding position in another. Where tracks carry presentation-timed access units, Group
> boundaries SHOULD be placed at the nearest access unit at or after the corresponding position in
> the track carrying the PCR, and matching Group numbers SHOULD correspond to positions within one
> access unit of each other. This requirement does not apply to tracks carrying signalling tables or
> other data without presentation timestamps; a subscriber combining such a track MUST use the
> presentation timestamps carried in the track payload, or the arrival order of its sections, to place
> its content.

And in §8, correspondingly, that the subscriber aligns on presentation position rather than on an
identical starting group number.

More fundamentally, and offered as a question rather than a proposal: MOQT Group IDs may be the wrong
synchronisation primitive here. They index a publisher's grouping decisions, which for good reasons
differ per track. A subscriber needs a shared *time* reference, and MSF's Media Timeline — which §5.6
already cites for PCR wrap-around, and §8 already mentions for resolving a time bound to a Group
location — looks like a better fit than group numbering for this purpose.

---

issues.title: Output timing is unspecified, so two conforming subscribers can produce differently-timed streams
issues.author: t0ms
issues.body:
> Context: one of a set of separate follow-ups to #7, from evaluating m2ts packaging for broadcast **primary distribution / contribution handed off to hardware IRDs** (SRT/Zixi/RIST-style satellite replacement). This round is prompted by the published three-mode restructure of §5.5. Background: https://github.com/tdrapier-wbd/moq-mpegts-paper (public technical evaluation, not yet widely announced).

## The ask, first

Promote the non-normative note in §5.6 into a normative subsection placing an output-timing
obligation on **the subscriber producing a transport-stream output**, and state a target that a
deployment can be held to.

## What the draft has today

§5.6 closes with:

> Note: Hardware IRDs recover the mux clock from the rate at which PCR-bearing packets arrive, not
> only from their encoded values. MOQT does not guarantee that Object delivery preserves the
> inter-packet timing of the source stream. Deployments targeting such receivers should account for
> this constraint and may require a rate-controlled egress that re-paces packets according to the
> source mux rate.

Every clause of that is correct. But it is non-normative, its "should" is lowercase and therefore not
BCP 14, it is addressed to "deployments" rather than to a protocol role, and it sits in a subsection
about PCR rather than anywhere a subscriber implementer is told what to do. As guidance it is
complete; as a requirement it does not exist.

*(Disclosure: that note was added at my request, in
[#12](https://github.com/mondain/msfts/pull/12). I am asking for it to be strengthened because the
form it took turns out not to bind anything.)*

## Why a note is not enough

The draft is normative and detailed about byte-level carriage. It fixes the payload as whole source
packets, requires payload lengths to be integer multiples of `m2tsPacketSize`, requires sync-byte
validation per packet, forbids continuity-counter rewriting and PID remapping in unmodified
carriage, and gives §8 a numbered validation procedure. A reader is left in no doubt that byte
fidelity is a conformance property.

Time fidelity is left as a deployment note — and for MPEG-2 Systems the two are not separable (#24). A
transport stream's PCR values specify the times at which its bytes are intended to enter a decoder,
and ISO/IEC 13818-1 §2.4.2 expresses the T-STD's buffer constraints against that schedule; ISO/IEC
13818-9 and, for DVB, ETSI TR 101 290 give the tolerance within which real delivery must match it. A
byte-perfect stream emitted with arbitrary inter-packet spacing carries a schedule it does not meet.

The interoperability consequence is the one a format specification exists to prevent. Two
implementations can satisfy every requirement in this document, be handed identical catalogs and
identical objects, and produce outputs of which one passes a TR 101 290 Priority 1 check and the
other does not. Nothing in the document distinguishes them, so neither can be said to be wrong.

## What it costs in practice

These are our own measurements on one media-aware implementation. They are software conformance
figures: **nothing here has been graded on a hardware IRD or a professional analyser**, so they show
a wire that fails a software TR 101 290 P1 check, not a receiver failing to lock.

Ungroomed egress, measured at the wire on a cross-host internet path over a 198,389-packet window,
against a source with **no PCR interval above 40 ms anywhere in 600 s**:

| | Source | Ungroomed MoQ egress |
|---|---|---|
| PCR intervals above 40 ms | 0 % | **8.19 %** |
| Worst PCR interval | 24.95 ms | **319.94 ms** |
| PAT repetition | 8.04 /s | **2.51 /s** |
| Mux rate | 9,945,951 b/s CBR | **none** — null stuffing not carried |

The same lane with a rate-controlled egress in front of it, measured at the wire: **0 of 20,193 PCR
intervals above 40 ms** over 300 s, worst 30.1 ms; and across a 24.01 h continuous run, 0 of
5,947,298 above 40 ms, worst 30.08 ms.

So for this class of implementation the difference between "conforms to the draft" and "produces a
stream a software P1 check accepts" is the whole of the primary timing metric, and it is decided
entirely outside the specification. The mode can be implemented perfectly by two parties and neither
output be usable, because the deciding property is not in the mode definition.

*(These figures come from a media-aware lane that regenerates PSI and PCR rather than carrying them.
Modes 1 and 2 carry both, so their exposure is smaller — but not zero: carriage preserves the encoded
PCR values and not the intervals at which the packets carrying them arrive, which is the quantity
§5.6's note is about.)*

## Proposed change

A new subsection after §5.6. Suggested text:

> ### 5.8. Egress Timing
>
> MOQT delivery does not preserve the inter-packet arrival timing of the source stream. A subscriber
> that produces a transport-stream output therefore determines that output's timing itself, and the
> timing of that output is not a property of this packaging.
>
> Where the output is delivered to a receiver that recovers its system clock from packet arrival, the
> subscriber MUST emit the reconstructed packet stream on a schedule consistent with the Program
> Clock Reference values it carries, and SHOULD meet the PCR repetition and PCR accuracy limits of
> the delivery standard in use; for DVB delivery these are given in ETSI TR 101 290. Where such a
> subscriber reconstructs a constant-bit-rate output, it SHOULD use `m2tsMuxRate` (Section 6.9) as
> the stuffing target and the carried PCR as the timing reference.
>
> Where the output is not delivered to such a receiver — for example a file, a software decoder, or a
> downstream multiplexer that imposes its own timing — a subscriber SHOULD NOT re-pace its output.
> Re-pacing requires a buffer, and adds delivery latency equal to that buffer's depth, without
> providing any property the consumer of the output uses.
>
> Which of these applies is a property of the consumer of the output and not of the track, so a
> subscriber that may serve both SHOULD make the behaviour configurable rather than inferring it.

### Why a conditional MUST rather than a SHOULD

Because within the condition there is no partial credit. If the receiver derives its clock from
arrival and the output is not paced, it does not work; there is no degraded-but-serviceable mode to
leave room for. That is the standard shape for a conditional MUST — *if you do X, you MUST do Y* — and
a SHOULD here would be worth very little, since it would trade the lowercase "should" of a
non-normative note for an uppercase one in a subsection and leave two conforming implementations
still indistinguishable.

The MUST also does not rest on my measurements. That a receiver of this kind requires it follows from
the base specifications and from §5.6's own existing note; my measurements show only that the gap
between the two is real in a current implementation. If the figures above were withdrawn entirely,
the requirement would stand unchanged.

### Why the SHOULD NOT matters as much as the MUST

The obvious objection to mandating output pacing is that pacing is frequently the wrong thing to do,
and that objection is correct. Re-pacing costs latency equal to the buffer it needs, and the cost is
not small: in this campaign the same media-aware lane measures a median delivery latency of
**109 ms** ungroomed and non-conformant (cross-host over the public internet) against **2,447 ms**
through a rate-controlled egress that does satisfy P1 (loopback, so if anything flattered on
transit). Those two figures come from different topologies and different configurations and no
deployment has both — which is the point: the conformant output costs more than two seconds of
latency that the non-conformant one does not. Mandating
pacing for every transport-stream output would make the format markedly worse for every consumer that
does not need it — a file writer, a software decoder, or a downstream multiplexer that will impose its
own rate and for which pacing twice adds latency and jitter for nothing.

So the requirement has to be narrow, and saying plainly where it does *not* apply is what makes it
narrow. That is also why the last paragraph asks for configurability rather than inference: nothing
in the catalog tells a subscriber what its output is for, and nothing should — the property belongs
to the deployment.

## What this does not ask for

Not a pacing algorithm, and not a profile. Getting re-pacing right is genuinely hard and is properly
an implementation matter — in our own work the variables that decided the outcome were PCR slot
pre-emption, the rate estimator, and whether the egress was clocked on the stream or on arrival,
the last of which is the difference between byte-identical dual outputs and 30–53 % alignment. The
parameter an implementer reaches for first, buffer depth, turned out not to be the variable at all.
A specification that states the target and leaves the method open is both the right scope and, for
anyone building such a component, the more useful outcome: it establishes that the component is
required, without constraining how it is built.

---
